title: Yama comes himself
hookLine: Savitri walks into the forest beside Satyavan on the day itself, and Death comes for him in person
carry: the body dies; the self is not slain

lines: AN AXE AND A FOREST PATH.
cards: Satyavan shoulders his axe. He's heading into the woods for fruit and firewood, as he does every morning. And Savitri, who has eaten nothing through her vow, asks to come along.
He's surprised. You've never come before, he says; the path is hard, and you're weak from fasting. She won't be talked out of it.
She even asks his parents' leave, and they give it. So the two of them set off together, and the epic says she looks cheerful while her heart is burning.

teach.b: Satyavan shows her the forest as they walk, the streams and the flowering trees. He gathers fruit and starts to split wood. Then he stops.
His head aches, he says. He wants to lie down. Savitri sits on the ground and takes his head into her lap.

teach.h: A DARK FIGURE WITH A NOOSE.
teach.b: And then she sees someone: a tall figure, dark, dressed in red, a noose in his hand, standing over Satyavan. She lays her husband's head down gently, stands, joins her palms and asks who he is.
He is Yama, lord of death, and Satyavan's time has come. Why have you come yourself, she asks, and not your messengers? Because Satyavan was good, Yama answers, not someone to be fetched by servants.
And with his noose he draws out of Satyavan's body a person no bigger than a thumb. Now the teaching in that detail.

teach.h: A PERSON THE SIZE OF A THUMB.
teach.b: The Upanishads describe the self within each of us as a person the size of a thumb. What Yama takes is not the body; the body lies still on the ground. What leaves is the self, the one who lived in it.

teach.h: THE BODY DIES; THE SELF IS NOT SLAIN.
teach.b: This is the Hindu view of death: the body dies, and the self is not slain.
The Bhagavad Gita says it plainly: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body and takes another.
And Yama is also called Dharmaraja, king of dharma: in this tradition, death keeps a just order. So Yama turns south with what he's taken.
And Savitri does what no one does. She follows. For today: when someone dies, Hindus grieve, and also hold this: the one we loved was never only the body.

how: In the Mahabharata's telling, Yama comes for Satyavan in person and draws out a thumb-sized person with his noose, the self the Upanishads describe; the Bhagavad Gita teaches that the self is not slain when the body is.

a messenger of the gods who carries the dead

s: Yama sent his messengers to fetch Satyavan
he came himself, he says, because Satyavan was so good.
in the story, Yama carries off Satyavan's body
the body stays on the ground. Yama draws out a person the size of a thumb, the self.
Satyavan was surprised that Savitri wanted to come into the woods
he reminds her she has never come before and is weak from fasting.

games.q: a friend's grandmother has died, and he asks what Hindus believe happens. by Savitri's story and the Gita, what fits?
o: the body dies, but the self isn't slain; it leaves the body like worn-out clothes.
nothing; death is the end of everything.
the body is carried off to Yama's city.
games.why: Yama draws out the thumb-sized self and the body stays behind. the Gita: the self is not slain when the body is slain.

practice: Many Hindus, remembering someone who has died, say om shanti: peace. Bring to mind someone you've lost, and let one good memory of them come back.
Then, if you pray, say om shanti softly three times for them; if not, simply wish them peace, wherever they are, and stay with the memory a while.

wordCard.voice: Yama. Lord of death, called Dharmaraja, king of dharma, who takes the self and leaves the body, and finds Savitri following.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Yama, lord of death and of dharma, who comes for Satyavan himself.

carryVoice: Your line: the body dies; the self is not slain. And Savitri isn't done. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Markandeya's story of Savitri): the walk into the forest; Satyavan's headache; the coming of Yama; the thumb-sized person drawn out with the noose
Katha Upanishad 2.1.12-13 (the person the size of a thumb, dwelling within the body)
Bhagavad Gita 2.20 and 2.22 (the self is not slain when the body is slain; as worn-out clothes are cast off; paraphrased)
